title-group.article-title: Resistance Training for Strength and Hypertrophy: A Practical Review

abstract.p: This sample article summarizes evidence on resistance training variables.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Resistance training is the primary stimulus for increasing muscular strength and size. Adaptations depend on how training variables — load, volume, frequency, and proximity to failure — are manipulated over time. Progressive overload, the gradual increase of mechanical demand, remains the organizing principle behind effective programs. This review outlines practical recommendations for the deadlift, squat, and press, and how to structure sets and repetitions for different goals.

Beginners typically respond to a wide range of loads, whereas trained individuals require more deliberate progression and higher relative intensities to continue adapting. Individual response varies, so programs should be adjusted based on recovery and performance trends rather than followed rigidly.

sec.title: Load and Repetition Ranges
sec.p: Strength is most effectively developed with heavy loads, roughly 80 to 95 percent of one repetition maximum, performed for one to five repetitions per set. Hypertrophy, or muscle growth, responds to a broader spectrum of loads, commonly six to twelve repetitions, provided sets are taken close to failure. The deadlift, a hip-hinge movement loading the posterior chain, is typically trained in lower repetition ranges because of its high systemic fatigue cost.

Repetitions in reserve — the number of additional repetitions one could perform at the end of a set — is a useful gauge of effort. Working with one to three repetitions in reserve balances stimulus against fatigue for most trainees.

sec.title: Training Volume and Frequency
sec.p: Weekly volume, often counted as the number of hard sets per muscle group, is a primary driver of hypertrophy. Ten to twenty sets per muscle group per week suits most trainees, distributed across two or more sessions. Higher frequencies allow the same weekly volume to be spread into smaller, better-quality sessions.

Recovery between sessions targeting the same movement should allow performance to be maintained or improved. Insufficient recovery manifests as stalled loads, reduced repetition counts, and persistent soreness.

sec.title: Deadlift Technique and Safety
sec.p: The conventional deadlift begins with the bar over the mid-foot and the shins nearly vertical. Bracing the trunk before the pull protects the spine by increasing intra abdominal pressure. The lifter takes the slack out of the bar, then drives the floor away as the hips and shoulders rise together, keeping the bar close to the body.

Rounding of the lower back under heavy load increases injury risk and should be avoided. Individuals with a history of back pain may prefer trap-bar or Romanian variations, which alter the loading on the lumbar spine while still training the posterior chain.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Effective resistance training applies progressive overload through appropriate load, volume, and frequency, individualized to recovery. Heavy compound movements such as the deadlift build strength efficiently when technique is sound and fatigue is managed.
